## Overview

The paper's question is how fast the environment can change before a population that
adapts to it genetically goes extinct [@Pagel2025]. Genetic change is not the only way to
keep up: an individual can respond to the environment it develops in. Phenotypic
plasticity is the standard reason a population might track an optimum that moves faster
than its genes can follow, and the standard theory of how much it helps, and what it costs,
is that of @Chevin2010 for a linear reaction norm, with the evolution of the norm itself
treated by @Lande2009.

QTLSim has a linear reaction norm (Julia only, off by default). This vignette shows where
it sits in the life cycle, an exact correspondence that makes a plastic population with a
perfect cue and no cost a slower-moving non-plastic one, what that means for the rate a
population can sustain (from a pre-specified experiment of 12,320 kernel runs, read from its
cache), the trade-off a cost of plasticity creates, the evolution of a heritable slope, and
what a delayed cue does under a fluctuating optimum.

A caution on sources. The formulas in QTLSim are derived from its own moments recursion,
`ḡ′ = ḡ + β (θ_t − ḡ − (b/B) θ_{t−τ})`, and checked symbolically
(`validate/symbolic/check_plasticity.jl`); the equations of @Chevin2010 were not read
(they are images in the article), so this vignette does not claim to reproduce them. Only
their qualitative statements were checked: the critical rate rises as `|B − b|` falls, a
cost lowers the population's growth, and above a threshold cost an intermediate
plasticity is best. The design note
[Phenotypic plasticity](https://ecorecipes.github.io/QTLSim.jl/dev/plasticity_design/)
gives the details.

## Setup

```{julia}
using QTLSim
import Catlab                                # loads the categorical layer, for run_moments
using CairoMakie, Printf, Random, Statistics
CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")
L = lifecycle(); g = L.generation            # QTSim's generation, Zygotes → Zygotes
```

## A reaction norm of fixed slope

The environment `ε` is measured by the optimum it sets, `θ = B ε`, with `B`
(`OptimumSlope`, 1 by default) the environmental sensitivity of selection. An individual's
phenotype is

$$z = g + b\,\varepsilon_{\text{cue}} + e, \qquad \varepsilon_{\text{cue}} = \theta_{t-\tau}/B,$$

with slope `b` (`Plasticity`), and a cue that is the environment `τ` (`CueLag`) generations
before selection; `τ = 0` is a perfect cue. A cost of plasticity is stabilising selection
on the slope: every fitness is multiplied by `exp(−b²/(2ω_b²))`, `ω_b = PlasticityCostSD`
(`Inf`, no cost, by default). For a fixed slope only the ratio `φ = b/B` matters: the plastic
part of the phenotype, `φ θ_{t−τ}`, is the fraction of the optimum's displacement that is
tracked without any genetic change.

Where is it expressed? In QTSim's generation the optimum of generation `t` is set in
`select`, after `develop` has formed the phenotypes (QTSim's `PopFitness`: phenotypes,
then the move, then fitness). The environment a perfect cue reports is not known when
`develop` runs, so `develop` is unchanged (it gives `g + e`, the phenotype in the reference
environment) and `select` moves the optimum, then expresses the norm, then computes
fitness. The plasticity fields are parameters of `select`:

```{julia}
step_schema(OneTraitModel())[:select]
```

so a `select` step can carry its own slope and cost, and demes can differ in them:

```{julia}
gp = withparams(g; Plasticity = 0.5, PlasticityCostSD = 1.0)
```

Only optima with a trajectory of their own are allowed: `:continuous`, `:red_noise`,
`:periodic`, or a step's fixed `θ`. QTSim's default `:phenotype` move (and `:fitness`)
re-anchors the optimum to the current mean phenotype every generation, `θ = z̄ + lead`, so
a plastic shift of the mean would be carried along by the optimum and have no meaning:

```{julia}
try
    World(Params(Plasticity = 0.5, MoveType = :phenotype, MoveFitnessSDGen = 100))
catch err
    println(sprint(showerror, err))
end
```

## An exact correspondence

With a perfect cue and no cost,

$$z - \theta = g + e - (1 - \varphi)\,\theta,$$

so fitness depends on the genotype and the optimum only through `(1 − φ) θ`. A plastic
population whose optimum moves `k` per generation is therefore, in distribution and not
only at steady state, a non-plastic population whose optimum moves `(1 − φ) k`. In the
kernel it is more than that: for the same seed the two runs draw the same random numbers
and make the same decisions. The parameters below are the 100-locus set of the experiment
in the next section (rare mutations, as in the paper's inputs), with a shorter burn-in:

```{julia}
p = Params(PopSize = 1000, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = 100, PhenotypeVar = 0.03, Heritability = 0.4,
           MutationScalar = 0.005, MutationRatePerGamete = 1e-4, InitFitnessSD = 4.0,
           RecombPoissonMean = 3.0, MoveType = :continuous, NoGenerations = 3000,
           MoveFitnessSDGen = 1000, MoveFitnessSD = 0.02)
plastic = simulate(Params(p; Plasticity = 0.5); seed = 1)            # φ = 0.5, k = 0.02
slower  = simulate(Params(p; MoveFitnessSD = 0.01); seed = 1)       # φ = 0,   k = 0.01
lag(o) = o.theta .- o.pheno_mean
@printf("survivors identical in every generation: %s\n", plastic.nsurv == slower.nsurv)
@printf("genetic variance identical in every generation: %s\n", plastic.geno_var == slower.geno_var)
@printf("largest difference in the lag θ − z̄: %.1e\n", maximum(abs.(lag(plastic) .- lag(slower))))
@printf("optimum at the end: %.2f (plastic) and %.2f (slower)\n", plastic.theta[end], slower.theta[end])
```

The optimum of the plastic run is twice as far away, its mean phenotype too, and
everything genetic is identical. Theory says the same: the steady lag behind a trend is
`(1 − φ) k (V_G + V_s)/V_G` (`steady_lag`), and `sustainable_rate`, the largest rate at
which the deterministic moments recursion persists (mean fitness at the steady lag above
`Ploidy/PopSize` at a fixed size, `1/R` under Beverton–Holt), is the rate without
plasticity divided by `1 − φ`:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
win = findall(t -> 2000 <= t <= 2999, plastic.gen)
VG = mean(plastic.geno_var[win])
println("| | kernel lag, generations 2000–2999 | `steady_lag` at the kernel's V_G | `sustainable_rate` |\n|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
for (nm, o, q) in (("φ = 0.5, k = 0.02", plastic, Params(p; Plasticity = 0.5)),
                   ("φ = 0, k = 0.01", slower, Params(p; MoveFitnessSD = 0.01)),
                   ("φ = 0, k = 0.02", nothing, p))
    @printf("| %s | %s | %.3f | %.4f |\n", nm, o === nothing ? "" : @sprintf("%.3f", mean(lag(o)[win])),
            steady_lag(q; VG), sustainable_rate(q; VG))
end
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
sl = steady_lag(Params(p; Plasticity = 0.5); VG)
@printf("The kernel's lag, %.2f (%.1f phenotypic standard deviations), is %.0f%% of the deterministic steady lag at its own V_G (%.2f), and it is the same for the plastic and the slower population. ",
        mean(lag(plastic)[win]), mean(lag(plastic)[win]) / sqrt(mean(plastic.pheno_var[win])),
        100 * mean(lag(plastic)[win]) / sl, sl)
println("The rest of the vignette is about what can break the correspondence: a cost, a heritable slope, and a cue that is out of date.")
```

## Survival against the rate of change

`validate/plasticity_rates.jl` is a pre-specified experiment (criteria written before the
first run, in the script's header) on the rate a population can sustain. Two synthetic
parameter sets within the paper's priors, with 100 and 500 loci (`L100`, `L500`), 1000
diploids, 10,000 generations of stabilising selection, then a continuous move; QTSim's
fixed size and Beverton–Holt with `R = 2`; `b/B` = 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 with a perfect cue,
without a cost and with `ω_b = 0.5`; eleven rates per cell; 40 burn-ins per cell; a run
survives if it is alive 2000 generations after the move. Without a cost one burn-in serves
all four slopes (the optimum is at the origin before the move, so the plastic part is
exactly zero), and the rates are chosen so that the *effective* rates `(1 − b/B) k` are the
same in every cell. Its 12,320 runs took about 10 hours; this vignette reads them from
`validate/plasticity_rates.csv`.

```{julia}
csv = joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "..", "validate", "plasticity_rates.csv")
lines_ = readlines(csv)
hdr = Symbol.(split(lines_[1], ','))
runs = map(lines_[2:end]) do l
    f = split(l, ',')
    (set = Symbol(f[1]), dem = Symbol(f[2]), cost = f[3] == "true", b = parse(Float64, f[4]),
     rep = parse(Int, f[5]), rate = parse(Float64, f[6]), keff = parse(Float64, f[7]),
     alive = f[8] == "false", vg0 = parse(Float64, f[10]), n0 = parse(Int, f[11]))
end
cell(set, dem, cost, b) = filter(r -> r.set == set && r.dem == dem && r.cost == cost && r.b == b, runs)
SETS, DEMS, SLOPES = (:L100, :L500), (:fixed, :bh), (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75)
length(runs)
```

The half-survival rate `k50` of a cell is the script's estimator: a maximum-likelihood
logistic regression of survival on `ln k` over the cell's eleven rates, `k50 = exp(−a/c)`.

```{julia}
function logistic(x, y)                      # logit P(y) = a + c x, by Newton's method
    a, c = 0.0, 0.0
    xm = mean(x); xc = x .- xm
    for _ in 1:100
        q = 1 ./ (1 .+ exp.(-clamp.(a .+ c .* xc, -30, 30)))
        g1, g2 = sum(y .- q), sum((y .- q) .* xc)
        w = q .* (1 .- q) .+ 1e-9
        h11, h12, h22 = sum(w), sum(w .* xc), sum(w .* xc .^ 2)
        d = h11 * h22 - h12^2
        da, dc = (h22 * g1 - h12 * g2) / d, (h11 * g2 - h12 * g1) / d
        s = min(1.0, 5 / max(abs(da), abs(dc), 1e-12))
        a += s * da; c += s * dc
        max(abs(da), abs(dc)) < 1e-10 && break
    end
    (a - c * xm, c)
end
function k50(rs)
    y = [r.alive for r in rs]
    (all(y) || !any(y)) && return NaN       # survival does not cross one half in the grid
    a, c = logistic([log(r.rate) for r in rs], y)
    c < 0 ? exp(-a / c) : NaN
end
survival(rs) = (ks = sort(unique(r.rate for r in rs));
                (ks, [mean(r.alive for r in rs if r.rate == k) for k in ks]))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-survival
#| fig-cap: "Survival 2000 generations after the move against the rate of change of the optimum, 40 populations per point. Top: against the rate k itself; bottom: against the effective rate (1 − b/B)k, as multiples of the half-survival rate without plasticity. Solid lines: no cost; dashed: cost ω_b = 0.5. Columns: the 100- and 500-locus parameter sets, at a fixed size and under Beverton–Holt with R = 2. Without a cost the four curves of the bottom row coincide, as the correspondence requires."
fig = Figure(size = (1000, 560))
cols = Makie.wong_colors()
titles = Dict((:L100, :fixed) => "L100, fixed size", (:L100, :bh) => "L100, Beverton–Holt",
              (:L500, :fixed) => "L500, fixed size", (:L500, :bh) => "L500, Beverton–Holt")
for (j, (set, dem)) in enumerate([(s, d) for s in SETS for d in DEMS])
    k0 = k50(cell(set, dem, false, 0.0))
    ax1 = Axis(fig[1, j], xscale = log10, title = titles[(set, dem)], xlabel = "rate k",
               ylabel = j == 1 ? "survival" : "")
    ax2 = Axis(fig[2, j], xlabel = "(1 − b/B) k / k50(0)", ylabel = j == 1 ? "survival" : "")
    for (i, b) in enumerate(SLOPES), cost in (false, true)
        (cost && b == 0) && continue
        rs = cell(set, dem, cost, b)
        isempty(rs) && continue
        ks, s = survival(rs)
        st = cost ? :dash : :solid
        lines!(ax1, ks, s, color = cols[i], linestyle = st, label = cost ? nothing : "b/B = $b")
        lines!(ax2, (1 - b) .* ks ./ k0, s, color = cols[i], linestyle = st)
    end
    j == 4 && Legend(fig[3, :], [[LineElement(color = cols[i]) for i in 1:4]; [LineElement(color = :black, linestyle = st) for st in (:solid, :dash)]],
                       [["b/B = $b" for b in SLOPES]; ["no cost", "cost ω_b = 0.5"]], orientation = :horizontal, framevisible = false)
end
fig
```

The top row shows what plasticity buys: the curves move to the right, by more the larger
the slope. The bottom row shows why: without a cost (solid lines) survival depends on the
effective rate only. The half-survival rates against the prediction `1/(1 − b/B)`
(criterion P1: within 15%):

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("| cell | k50, b = 0 | b/B = 0.25 | b/B = 0.5 | b/B = 0.75 |\n|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
println("| predicted ratio `1/(1 − b/B)` | | 1.333 | 2.000 | 4.000 |")
K0 = Dict((s, d) => k50(cell(s, d, false, 0.0)) for s in SETS for d in DEMS)
for set in SETS, dem in DEMS
    @printf("| %s | %.4f | %s |\n", titles[(set, dem)], K0[(set, dem)],
            join((@sprintf("%.3f", k50(cell(set, dem, false, b)) / K0[(set, dem)]) for b in SLOPES[2:end]), " | "))
end
```

All twelve cells pass, within 2% of the prediction (the log's 95% bootstrap intervals are
within 1.32–1.38, 1.95–2.07 and 3.93–4.13). That is a check of the implementation, not a
test of a theory: the correspondence above is exact, so it must hold whatever the genetics.
The lag at equal effective rates (criterion P3) passes in all twelve cells too.

### With a cost

With `ω_b = 0.5` every fitness is multiplied by `plasticity_cost`, 0.88, 0.61 and 0.32 for
the three slopes, and the correspondence is broken. The pre-specified prediction (P2) was
the ratio of `sustainable_rate` with and without the cost, evaluated at each cell's mean
`V_G` at the move, to within 25%; under Beverton–Holt at `b/B = 0.75` the prediction is that
the population dies before the move (`R W̄(0) = 2 × 0.997 × 0.32 < 1`).

```{julia}
#| output: asis
base(set, dem) = Params(; PopSize = 1000, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = set == :L100 ? 100 : 500, RecombPoissonMean = 3.0,
                        PhenotypeVar = set == :L100 ? 0.03 : 0.05, Heritability = set == :L100 ? 0.4 : 0.3,
                        MutationScalar = set == :L100 ? 0.005 : 0.008, MutationRatePerGamete = 1e-4,
                        InitFitnessSD = set == :L100 ? 4.0 : 3.0, MoveType = :continuous,
                        (dem == :bh ? (Demography = :beverton_holt, GrowthRate = 2.0) : (;))...)
meanfin(v) = (w = filter(isfinite, collect(v)); isempty(w) ? NaN : mean(w))
println("| cell | b/B | V_G at the move, no cost | with cost | N at the move, with cost | burn-ins dead | k50 ratio, observed | predicted | observed/predicted | P2 |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|")
p2 = Dict{Any,String}()
for set in SETS, dem in DEMS, b in SLOPES[2:end]
    p0 = base(set, dem)
    v0 = mean(r.vg0 for r in cell(set, dem, false, 0.0))
    rs = cell(set, dem, true, b)
    vc = meanfin(r.vg0 for r in rs)
    nc = mean(r.n0 for r in rs)
    dead = mean(r.n0 == 0 for r in rs)
    pred = sustainable_rate(Params(p0; Plasticity = b, PlasticityCostSD = 0.5); VG = isfinite(vc) ? vc : v0) /
           sustainable_rate(p0; VG = v0)
    obs = k50(rs) / K0[(set, dem)]
    v = pred == 0 ? (dead >= 0.9 ? "PASS" : "FAIL") : (isfinite(obs) && 0.75 <= obs / pred <= 1.25 ? "PASS" : "FAIL")
    p2[(set, dem, b)] = v
    @printf("| %s | %.2f | %.4f | %s | %.0f | %.0f%% | %s | %.3f | %s | %s |\n", titles[(set, dem)], b, v0,
            isfinite(vc) ? @sprintf("%.4f", vc) : "–", nc, 100dead,
            isfinite(obs) ? @sprintf("%.3f", obs) : (pred == 0 ? "–" : "below 0.63"), pred,
            isfinite(obs) && pred > 0 ? @sprintf("%.2f", obs / pred) : "–", v)
end
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
@printf("P2 passes in %d of 12 cells and fails in %d, as in `validate/plasticity_rates.log`. ",
        count(==("PASS"), values(p2)), count(==("FAIL"), values(p2)))
println("At a fixed size the cost is less harmful than predicted, increasingly so at larger slopes (observed/predicted up to 1.39), and the two fixed-size cells at `b/B = 0.75` fail on that side. ",
        "Under Beverton–Holt at `b/B = 0.5` every population died even at the lowest rate of the grid, so the half-survival rate is not bracketed (it is below 0.63 of `k50(0)`); ",
        "the grid had been placed using the nominal `V_G`, and the prediction with the realised `V_G`, 0.29–0.36, lies below it, in the same direction as the observation.")
```

What the table shows directly is that the cost lowers the genetic variance at the move,
before the optimum has moved at all: by 5–58% at a fixed size and by 15–72% under
Beverton–Holt, where the population also shrinks (to about 340 at `b/B = 0.5`). That this
is *why* P2 fails is an inference made after the run, not a pre-specified test: fewer
survivors per generation means more drift, and a smaller population more still, and the
prediction allowed for the lower `V_G` but not for how the half-survival rate responds to
it (at a fixed size the deterministic threshold is 5–7 times the observed `k50`, and `k50`
responds less than proportionally to `V_G`). No model or criterion was changed after the
run, and no fresh-seed confirmation was made.

## The cost trade-off

Without a cost, more plasticity is always better, and at `b = B` the population tracks the
optimum without any genetic change. A cost changes that. At the steady lag the mean fitness
is

$$\bar W(\lambda) = c\, e^{-b^2/(2\omega_b^2)}\,\frac{\omega}{\sqrt{s}}\, e^{-\lambda^2/(2s)},\qquad s = \omega^2 + V_G + V_E,$$

and the largest sustainable rate is

$$k_{\max} = \frac{V_G}{s}\,\frac{\sqrt{2s\,\big(\ln(\bar W_0/W_{\min}) - b^2/(2\omega_b^2)\big)}}{|1 - b/B|},$$

with `W̄₀` the mean fitness at no lag without a cost and `W_min` the threshold: `Ploidy/N`
at a fixed size, `1/R` under Beverton–Holt (`sustainable_rate`). Plasticity divides the
rate the genotype must supply by `1 − b/B`, and the cost eats into the logarithmic
"headroom" `ln(W̄₀/W_min)`. When the headroom is large the gain wins up to large slopes;
when it is small the cost wins early, and an intermediate slope is best. A fixed size of
1000 diploids has a headroom of `ln(500 W̄₀) ≈ 6`; Beverton–Holt with `R = 2` has
`ln(2 W̄₀) ≈ 0.7`. `plasticity_cost` gives the factor:

```{julia}
pc = Params(base(:L100, :fixed); PlasticityCostSD = 0.5)
[plasticity_cost(pc; b) for b in SLOPES]
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-tradeoff
#| fig-cap: "The sustainable rate with plasticity relative to that without, against the slope b/B, for the 100-locus set at a fixed size (left) and under Beverton–Holt with R = 2 (right), at the V_G of the populations without a cost. Lines: sustainable_rate for no cost and three costs; small dots mark the best slope where it lies below B. Points: the experiment's half-survival rates relative to b = 0, without a cost (open) and with ω_b = 0.5 (filled); under Beverton–Holt the populations with cost at b/B = 0.5 all died at the lowest rate tried (plotted at that bound, triangle) and at 0.75 before the move (plotted at 0)."
bs = range(0, 0.95, 200)
fig = Figure(size = (900, 380))
for (j, dem) in enumerate(DEMS)
    p0 = base(:L100, dem)
    v0 = mean(r.vg0 for r in cell(:L100, dem, false, 0.0))
    r0 = sustainable_rate(p0; VG = v0)
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j], xlabel = "b/B", ylabel = j == 1 ? "rate relative to b = 0" : "", yscale = log10,
              title = dem == :fixed ? "fixed size" : "Beverton–Holt, R = 2")
    for (i, ωb) in enumerate((Inf, 1.0, 0.5, 0.25))
        r = [sustainable_rate(Params(p0; PlasticityCostSD = ωb); VG = v0, b) / r0 for b in bs]
        ok = r .> 0
        lines!(ax, bs[ok], r[ok], color = cols[i], label = isinf(ωb) ? "no cost" : "ω_b = $ωb")
        isinf(ωb) || (m = argmax(r); m < length(bs) && scatter!(ax, [bs[m]], [r[m]], color = cols[i]))
    end
    scatter!(ax, collect(SLOPES[2:end]), [k50(cell(:L100, dem, false, b)) / K0[(:L100, dem)] for b in SLOPES[2:end]],
             color = :white, strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1.5, markersize = 10)
    obs = [k50(cell(:L100, dem, true, b)) / K0[(:L100, dem)] for b in SLOPES[2:end]]
    for (b, o) in zip(SLOPES[2:end], obs)
        if isfinite(o)
            scatter!(ax, [b], [o], color = cols[3], strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1, markersize = 10)
        elseif dem == :bh && b == 0.5
            scatter!(ax, [b], [0.63], marker = :dtriangle, color = cols[3], strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1, markersize = 12)
        end
    end
    ylims!(ax, 0.2, 12)
    j == 1 && axislegend(ax, position = :lt, framevisible = false)
end
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
best(dem, ωb) = (p0 = base(:L100, dem); v0 = mean(r.vg0 for r in cell(:L100, dem, false, 0.0));
                 bs[argmax([sustainable_rate(Params(p0; PlasticityCostSD = ωb); VG = v0, b) for b in bs])])
@printf("At a fixed size a cost of `ω_b = 0.5` never uses up the headroom before `b = B` (`b²/(2ω_b²) < 2`), so the sustainable rate still grows without bound as the slope approaches `B`; with `ω_b = 0.25` the best slope is %.2f. Under Beverton–Holt, with a headroom of about 0.7, a cost of `ω_b = 1` still leaves the rate unbounded (`b²/2 < 0.5`), but `ω_b = 0.5` puts the best slope at %.2f and `ω_b = 0.25` at %.2f. ", best(:fixed, 0.25), best(:bh, 0.5), best(:bh, 0.25))
println("The experiment agrees in direction. At a fixed size the half-survival rate with the cost rose with the slope across the grid (1.24, 1.46 and 2.11 times that at `b = 0` for the 100-locus set), more than the prediction. ",
        "Under Beverton–Holt the slope 0.25 helped a little (1.03 times), 0.5 was fatal at every rate tried, and 0.75 killed every population before the move: an intermediate plasticity is best, and the demography decides where.")
```

## A heritable reaction norm

With `ReactionNorm = true` and `NoTraits = 2` the slope is heritable: the two heritable
values of the model of several traits (vignette
[Several traits and pleiotropy](../13_multiple_traits/13_multiple_traits.qmd)) are the
elevation `a = g₁` and the deviation of the slope from `Plasticity`, `b = Plasticity + g₂`.
Selection acts on the one phenotype `z = a + b ε + e` and the cost on the individual's slope.
It is `TraitModel(2)` with a linear map `(a, b) ↦ a + b ε`, which changes with the
environment, composed before selection (`ReactionNormModel()`); the kernel and the moments
lowering have it, the Eidos lowering does not.

Without a cost the slope responds in proportion to `ε` (`reaction_norm_response`:
`Δ(ā, b̄) = G v λ/s`, `v = (1, ε)`), so it evolves only away from the reference
environment, and under a sustained move the mean slope approaches `B`. With a cost, in a
constant environment the only equilibrium has `b̄ = 0` [genetic assimilation, @Lande2009],
and under a sustained move the slope settles below `B`. The parameters are those of
`validate/reaction_norm.jl` (1000 diploids, 50 loci in the Gaussian regime, initial slope
0.2, 1000 generations of stabilising selection at `ε = 0`, then the optimum moves 0.02 per
generation for 1500 generations), with 8 runs per scenario instead of 40:

```{julia}
rn = Params(NoGenerations = 2500, PopSize = 1000, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = 50, MutationRatePerGamete = 0.01,
            MoveType = :continuous, MoveFitnessSDGen = 1000, MoveFitnessSD = 0.02, RecombPoissonMean = 3.0,
            InitFitnessSD = 1.0, PhenotypeVar = 1.0, Heritability = 0.5)
Vm = muteVar(rn)
norm_params(ωb) = Params(rn; NoTraits = 2, ReactionNorm = true, Plasticity = 0.2,
                         MutCov = [Vm 0.0; 0.0 Vm / 4], PlasticityCostSD = ωb)
scen = [("no cost", Inf), ("cost ω_b = 1", 1.0)]
njobs = [(i, r) for i in eachindex(scen) for r in 1:8]
nruns = Vector{Any}(undef, length(njobs))
Threads.@threads :greedy for j in eachindex(njobs)
    i, r = njobs[j]
    nruns[j] = simulate(norm_params(scen[i][2]); seed = 31_000 + 100i + r)
end
nmom = [run_moments(norm_params(ωb); erosion = true, loci = :multilocus) for (_, ωb) in scen]
kruns(i) = [nruns[j] for j in eachindex(njobs) if njobs[j][1] == i]
slope(o) = [m[2] for m in o.trait_mean]
nlag(o) = o.theta .- [m[1] for m in o.trait_mean]
Gbb(o) = [G[2, 2] for G in o.gmatrix];
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-norm
#| fig-cap: "A heritable reaction norm under a sustained move from generation 1000. Left: the mean slope; middle: the lag θ − z̄; right: the slope's genetic variance G_bb. Thin lines: each kernel run; thick: their mean; dashed black: the moments lowering (multilocus Gaussian with drift). Blue: no cost; orange: cost ω_b = 1. The optimum's slope on the environment is B = 1."
fig = Figure(size = (1000, 330))
axs = [Axis(fig[1, j], xlabel = "generation", title = t) for (j, t) in enumerate(("mean slope b̄", "lag θ − z̄", "G_bb"))]
for (i, (nm, _)) in enumerate(scen)
    rs = kruns(i)
    for (ax, f) in zip(axs, (slope, nlag, Gbb))
        for o in rs
            lines!(ax, 1:2500, f(o), color = (cols[i], 0.2), linewidth = 0.6)
        end
        lines!(ax, 1:2500, mean(f.(rs)), color = cols[i], linewidth = 2, label = nm)
        lines!(ax, 1:2500, f(nmom[i]), color = :black, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.2)
    end
end
hlines!(axs[1], [1.0], color = :grey, linestyle = :dot)
xlims!(axs[2], 900, 2500); ylims!(axs[2], -0.05, 0.4)
axislegend(axs[1], position = :rb, framevisible = false)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("| | mean slope, generation 1250 | 1500 | 2000 | 2500 | lag at 2500 |\n|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for (i, (nm, _)) in enumerate(scen)
    rs = kruns(i)
    @printf("| %s, kernel (8 runs) | %s | %.3f |\n", nm,
            join((@sprintf("%.3f", mean(slope(o)[t] for o in rs)) for t in (1250, 1500, 2000, 2500)), " | "),
            mean(mean(nlag(o)[2451:2500]) for o in rs))
    @printf("| %s, moments | %s | %.3f |\n", nm,
            join((@sprintf("%.3f", slope(nmom[i])[t]) for t in (1250, 1500, 2000, 2500)), " | "),
            mean(nlag(nmom[i])[2451:2500]))
end
```

Without a cost the mean slope climbs from 0.2 toward `B = 1` and the lag, after a peak
early in the move, falls toward zero: with heritable, cost-free plasticity this model has no
critical rate, only a transient. With the cost the slope is first drawn to zero during the
stationary phase (genetic assimilation), rises more slowly under the move and stays well
below `B`, and the lag stays larger. In both the slope's genetic variance is used up as the
slope responds. `validate/reaction_norm.jl` makes this comparison with 40 runs and passes
28 of its 30 pre-specified criteria; the two failures are the quasi-steady lag formula
(`reaction_norm_lag`) late in the cost-free move, where the lag has fallen to 0.003 and
below and the ratio is noise:

```{julia}

logf = joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "..", "validate", "reaction_norm.log")
if isfile(logf)
    for l in readlines(logf)
        (occursin("C2 FAIL", l) || occursin("criteria pass", l)) && println("    ", strip(l))
    end
end
```

## A delayed cue under a fluctuating optimum

A cue that is `τ` generations old makes no difference to the steady lag behind a trend: the
genotype makes up the constant shortfall. It matters when the optimum fluctuates. With red
noise (`MoveType = :red_noise`: an AR(1) optimum of standard deviation `σ`, autocorrelation
`ρ`) the lag with plasticity is `λ_t = L_t − φ L_{t−τ}`, with `L` the lag without
plasticity, so

$$\operatorname{Var}\lambda = (1 + \varphi^2)\,\Gamma(0) - 2\varphi\,\Gamma(\tau),$$

with `Γ` the autocovariance of `L` (`red_noise_lag_var` with `b`, `B` and `τ`;
`red_noise_lag_autocov`). A perfect cue scales the variance by `(1 − φ)²`; a cue so old
that the environment has forgotten it (`ρ^τ → 0`) makes plasticity add noise, `1 + φ²`
times the variance without plasticity. In between there is a delay at which plasticity
stops helping.

```{julia}
pr = Params(PopSize = 500, Ploidy = 2, NoQTL = 10, PhenotypeVar = 1.0, Heritability = 0.5,
            MutationScalar = 0.01, MutationRatePerGamete = 0.02, InitFitnessSD = 1.5,
            NoGenerations = 3000, MoveFitnessSDGen = 1000, MoveFitnessSD = 0.0,
            MoveType = :red_noise, MoveNoiseSD = 0.5, MoveAutocorr = 0.8)
φ = 0.6
τs = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12]
rjobs = [(b, τ, r) for (b, τ) in vcat([(0.0, 0)], [(φ, τ) for τ in τs]) for r in 1:6]
rres = Vector{Any}(undef, length(rjobs))
Threads.@threads :greedy for j in eachindex(rjobs)
    b, τ, r = rjobs[j]
    o = simulate(Params(pr; Plasticity = b, CueLag = τ); seed = 7000 + j)
    w = findall(t -> 1500 <= t <= 2999, o.gen)
    rres[j] = (; b, τ, lag2 = mean((o.theta[w] .- o.pheno_mean[w]) .^ 2), VG = mean(o.geno_var[w]))
end
Vs = selection_variance(pr)
VGk = mean(r.VG for r in rres)
th(b, τ) = red_noise_lag_var(pr.MoveNoiseSD, pr.MoveAutocorr; VG = VGk, Vs, b, τ)
obs(b, τ) = (v = [r.lag2 for r in rres if r.b == b && r.τ == τ]; (mean(v), std(v) / sqrt(length(v))));
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-cue
#| fig-cap: "The mean squared lag behind red noise (σ = 0.5, ρ = 0.8) with a reaction norm of slope b/B = 0.6, against the age τ of the cue. Line: red_noise_lag_var at the kernel's mean V_G; points: kernel, 6 runs each (mean ± SE over generations 1500–2999); grey: without plasticity, theory (dashed) and kernel (band, ± SE). Illustrative, not a pre-specified validation."
fig = Figure(size = (520, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "age of the cue τ (generations)", ylabel = "E[(θ − z̄)²]")
τf = 0:12
lines!(ax, τf, [th(φ, τ) for τ in τf], color = :crimson, label = "theory, b/B = $φ")
m0, s0 = obs(0.0, 0)
band!(ax, [0, 12], [m0 - s0, m0 - s0], [m0 + s0, m0 + s0], color = (:grey, 0.3))
hlines!(ax, [th(0.0, 0)], color = :grey, linestyle = :dash, label = "no plasticity")
hlines!(ax, [(1 + φ^2) * th(0.0, 0)], color = :grey, linestyle = :dot, label = "(1 + φ²) × no plasticity")
mo = [obs(φ, τ) for τ in τs]
errorbars!(ax, τs, first.(mo), last.(mo), color = :black, whiskerwidth = 6)
scatter!(ax, τs, first.(mo), color = :black, label = "kernel")
axislegend(ax, position = :rb, framevisible = false)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
τc = findfirst(τ -> th(φ, τ) > th(0.0, 0), τf)
@printf("With a perfect cue plasticity cuts the mean squared lag to %.3f from %.3f without (theory %.3f and %.3f). ",
        obs(φ, 0)[1], m0, th(φ, 0), th(0.0, 0))
@printf("Plasticity stops helping once the cue is %d generations old, and at 12 generations it is %.0f%% worse than none, beyond the limit `1 + φ²` (%.0f%% worse) for a very old cue, because the lag's autocovariance `Γ(12)` is negative: an old cue is anticorrelated with the present lag. ",
        τf[τc], 100 * (th(φ, 12) / th(0.0, 0) - 1), 100φ^2)
@printf("The kernel lies %.0f–%.0f%% above the deterministic theory: ",
        100 * minimum(first(obs(φ, τ)) / th(φ, τ) - 1 for τ in τs), 100 * maximum(first(obs(φ, τ)) / th(φ, τ) - 1 for τ in τs))
println("the theory leaves out the drift of the mean and the sampling error of the recorded mean, which add to the lag (as for several traits in vignette 13). ",
        "This is an illustration with a few runs, not a validation: a delayed cue has not been tested against the theory in a pre-specified experiment.")
```

The same holds for a periodic optimum, where `expected_lag2` multiplies the squared
amplitude of the lag by `1 + φ² − 2φ cos(2πτ/P)`: a cue half a period old doubles down on
the wrong phase. And `lag_load` adds the cost `b²/(2ω_b²)` to the load of the lag, so with
a cost and an unreliable cue the best slope is smaller still.

## Where next

- The cost's effect on the sustainable rate was predicted from the deterministic threshold
  at the realised `V_G`, and failed in 4 of 12 cells. A prediction that allows for the
  extra drift a cost causes, or for the spectrum of segregating mutations under a moving
  optimum (`run_moments(…; loci = :spectrum)`), has not been tried.
- A heritable norm under fluctuating environments is the setting of the plasticity-first
  and genetic-assimilation literature [@Lande2009]; the kernel and the moments lowering can
  run it, but nothing here has validated it, and it has no SLiM lowering.
- Not validated: a delayed cue in a pre-specified test, plasticity with fecundity
  selection, and plasticity in metapopulations with migration (a migrant expresses the
  norm in the deme it develops in; `withparams(g; Plasticity = …)` gives demes their own
  slopes).
